pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11. The K-Pg (Cretaceous–Paleogene) mass extinction ~66 Mya that ended the non-avian dinosaurs — taught as a DETECTIVE CASE built from converging physical evidence, not a told story.
• Standards — UK (DfE): no direct statutory KS2 dinosaur content; anchor to Y3 Rocks (fossils form when things living in rock are trapped) and Y6 Evolution & inheritance (fossils tell us about the past), plus 'asking scientific questions and using evidence to answer them' from the KS2 working-scientifically strand. Leads to KS3 Earth's history.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence of past organisms/environments) is the anchor; extends to MS-ESS1-4 (geologic time) and the nature-of-science idea that scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence.
• Operational details: build the argument in layers — (1) the worldwide clay layer rich in IRIDIUM, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids; (2) shocked quartz + tektites (melt droplets) that need enormous pressure; (3) a buried ~180 km crater at Chicxulub, Yucatán, same age as the layer; (4) drilling INTO the crater (2016) found the same iridium signature inside it, tying crater to global layer. Then the mechanism: dust/soot/sulfate aerosols blocked sunlight → impact winter → photosynthesis crashed → food chains collapsed.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (concrete, ~9): point to the special worldwide clay layer and say what it is made of and where it came from. Tier B (transitional, ~10): name two independent clues (iridium AND the crater) and explain why one clue alone is weaker than two. Tier C (formal, ~11): explain the causal CHAIN from impact → blocked sunlight → collapsed food chains, and note that a rival idea (Deccan Traps volcanism) exists — evidence, not authority, decides.
bestPractices: Frame it as evidence-to-conclusion detective work: present the clues (iridium, shocked quartz, crater) and let children infer the cause, rather than announcing 'an asteroid did it' first.
Emphasise CONVERGING independent lines of evidence — the strength is that chemistry, geology and the crater's age all point the same way; one clue alone would be weak.

Teach the mechanism as a causal chain (impact → dust/soot → sunlight blocked → plants die → herbivores → carnivores), so extinction is understood as ecosystem collapse, not direct killing by the blast.

Explicitly model nature-of-science: a rival hypothesis (Deccan Traps volcanism) still has supporters, and the impact case strengthened over decades as new evidence arrived — science is provisional and evidence-led.
Anchor deep time — 'birds are the dinosaurs that survived' — to avoid the total-annihilation misconception.
keyRepresentations: The K-Pg boundary rock column: dinosaur bones below, thin grey iridium clay layer, none above.
An iridium-vs-depth graph with a sharp spike at the boundary.
A world map with boundary sites all showing the same layer, converging on Chicxulub.
A food-web/energy-pyramid diagram going dark as sunlight is removed.
A before/after Cretaceous scene (thriving) vs impact-winter (dim, cold).
commonMisconceptions: 'The asteroid killed the dinosaurs on impact' — most died from the global aftermath (impact winter, food-chain collapse), not the blast itself.
'All dinosaurs died' — avian dinosaurs (birds) survived; dinosaurs are not entirely extinct.
'Dinosaurs and early humans overlapped' — ~66 My separate the extinction from humans.
'One clue proved it' — the case rests on multiple independent evidence lines, not a single discovery.
'Science has closed the book' — a genuine minority hypothesis (Deccan volcanism) persists; debate continues.

learn.summary: Teach the K-Pg mass extinction (~66 Mya, ending the non-avian dinosaurs) for ages 9-11 as evidence-to-conclusion detective work rather than a told story. Learners assemble converging independent clues (a worldwide iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites, the buried ~180 km Chicxulub crater, and iridium found inside the crater by drilling) and then reason through the causal chain: impact -> dust/soot/sulfate aerosols block sunlight -> impact winter -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores starve -> carnivores starve -> ecosystem collapse. Core nature-of-science goals: the strength of a case comes from multiple independent lines agreeing; a genuine rival hypothesis (Deccan Traps volcanism) persists and evidence, not authority, decides; and birds are surviving dinosaurs, so extinction was near-total, not total.

activities.title: Assemble the case file: what killed the dinosaurs?
feedback: If a learner says one discovery 'proved' it, point back to the case file: ask them to name a second independent clue and say what the case would look like with only one.
If a learner treats the crater and the clay layer as unrelated, direct them to the drill-core result — the same iridium signature inside the crater is what connects the two.
Affirm correct reasoning that iridium's rarity in the crust plus its abundance in asteroids is what makes a worldwide iridium layer surprising and meaningful.
If a learner cannot say why iridium is a clue, prompt: where is iridium common, and where is it rare?
activities.rationale: The target understanding is the reasoning move of gathering independent evidence and tying a local cause (crater) to a global effect (worldwide layer). Having learners collect and compare clues, rather than being told the answer first, makes that reasoning the thing they practise. An interactive map/assay format (measurement that spikes at the layer, a core-drill that reveals iridium inside the crater, a visual link joining crater to layer) can make the converging-evidence idea concrete; these interaction examples are optional illustrations of the mechanism, not required features.
sourceClaims: The Chicxulub crater (~180 km wide, Yucatán) was formed by an asteroid impact ~66 Mya at the end of the Cretaceous; the impact and resulting climate change caused a mass extinction that wiped out ~75–80% of species including the (non-avian) dinosaurs.

The asteroid hypothesis originated with Luis Alvarez's team finding unusually high iridium at the K–Pg boundary; iridium is rare in the crust (siderophile, sank to the core) but abundant in asteroids, and similar iridium spikes were found at the boundary worldwide.

Drilling into the crater (IODP-ICDP Expedition 364) found the iridium anomaly WITHIN the peak-ring sequence, conclusively tying Chicxulub to the global iridium layer and K-Pg boundary sections worldwide; lead author Steven Goderis: 'The circle is now finally complete.'

Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.
learnerActions: Open a 'case file' and visit several boundary sites on a world map (e.g. Italy, Denmark, New Zealand, and a land site such as Hell Creek in Montana, USA); at each, examine the rock column and find the thin clay band at the boundary. At land sites like Hell Creek, non-avian dinosaur fossils are found below the band and none above it; at old sea-floor sites like Italy and Denmark, many kinds of tiny sea fossils found below the band disappear above it.

Run an iridium measurement at each site and record where the reading spikes — notice the spike lands at the clay layer at each site you visit, and that similar spikes have been found at the boundary at many sites around the world.

State in your own words why iridium at this layer points to space: iridium is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, so a worldwide layer of it suggests material that fell from the sky everywhere at once.

Examine two more independent clues from a large impact: shocked quartz, which forms under the intense shock pressure of an impact, and tektites, which are droplets of rock melted and flung out by the impact's heat and energy — both are products of one large impact rather than both being pressure-formed.
Reveal the buried ~180 km Chicxulub crater in the Yucatan on a geophysics view, and check that its age matches the clay layer.
Drill a core into the crater and find the same iridium signature inside it; draw or describe the link that ties the crater to the global layer.
Write down which clues are independent and explain why two or more clues that agree make a stronger case than any single clue alone.
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific conclusion is built from converging independent evidence: chemistry (iridium), geology (shocked quartz, tektites, crater), and matching ages all point the same way, and drilling into the crater closed the link between the local crater and the global layer.

activities.title: Run the aftermath: trace the causal chain
feedback: If a learner says the asteroid burned or crushed all the dinosaurs, separate the local impact from the global aftermath: ask how a strike in Mexico could reach animals on the other side of the world, and lead them to the blocked-sunlight/food-chain route.
If a learner reverses the order (carnivores first), prompt: where does the food chain get its energy, and which group depends on plants most directly?
If a learner says every dinosaur died, note that non-avian dinosaurs died out but birds — living dinosaurs — survived.
Affirm answers that name the global 'impact winter' and food-chain collapse as the mechanism reaching the whole planet, supported by the worldwide iridium layer and the crater.
activities.rationale: A common misconception is that the impact killed dinosaurs directly; the discriminating idea is the indirect, global mechanism of blocked sunlight and food-chain collapse. Letting learners manipulate the sunlight and watch trophic levels fail in sequence makes causation something they trace rather than recite. The sunlight slider and sequential dimming are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.

The Chicxulub crater (~180 km wide, Yucatán) was formed by an asteroid impact ~66 Mya at the end of the Cretaceous; the impact and resulting climate change caused a mass extinction that wiped out ~75–80% of species including the (non-avian) dinosaurs.
learnerActions: Starting from a thriving Cretaceous scene, release the dust and soot from the impact and reduce incoming sunlight (for example, by lowering a sunlight slider) to model an 'impact winter'.
Observe and describe, in order, what happens as sunlight drops: plants dim and die, then plant-eaters (herbivores) starve, then meat-eaters (carnivores) that fed on them starve.
Explain in your own words why plant-eaters are affected before meat-eaters, using the idea that energy enters a food chain through plants/photosynthesis.
Write the full causal chain as a sequence: impact -> dust/soot/aerosols -> sunlight blocked -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.
State clearly that worldwide extinction came from these after-effects, not from the blast crushing or burning dinosaurs everywhere, and note that the impact itself mainly devastated the local area.
Add a note that birds are surviving dinosaurs, so the extinction was near-total, not total.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass extinction was caused by ecosystem collapse — blocked sunlight shutting down the food supply across the whole planet — rather than by the impact directly killing animals far from the crater; and survival of birds means dinosaurs are not entirely extinct.

activities.title: Weigh the rival hypothesis
feedback: If a learner thinks 'science has closed the book', note that a genuine minority hypothesis (Deccan volcanism) persists and that the impact case itself strengthened over time as evidence accumulated.

If a learner dismisses the rival outright, ask what the volcanism idea can explain (huge Deccan eruptions happened around the same time and could change the climate) and what evidence would help decide how much each cause mattered.
Affirm reasoning that cites specific converging evidence rather than appealing to who said it.
activities.rationale: Modelling nature-of-science explicitly — rival hypotheses, provisional knowledge, evidence over authority — is an anchor standard for this topic and guards against the misconception that the debate is settled or that one discovery decided it. A short discussion or interview with a researcher (e.g. asking why the iridium finding was surprising) can extend this, though the core work is weighing evidence.
sourceClaims: Impact evidence includes a global iridium-rich clay layer, shocked quartz and tektites; expedition found dust, sulfate aerosols and soot driving global cooling and reduced photosynthesis as extinction drivers; a rival Deccan Traps volcanism hypothesis (Gerta Keller) persists.

The asteroid hypothesis originated with Luis Alvarez's team finding unusually high iridium at the K–Pg boundary; iridium is rare in the crust (siderophile, sank to the core) but abundant in asteroids, and similar iridium spikes were found at the boundary worldwide.
learnerActions: Compare two explanations for the extinction: the asteroid impact and Deccan Traps volcanism, considering what each can explain and whether both might have played a part.
List which pieces of evidence (worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age crater, iridium inside the crater) fit the impact explanation.
Discuss or write why the impact case grew stronger over decades as new evidence arrived, and why a minority of scientists still support the volcanism idea.

Conclude with a statement about how scientists decide between rival ideas — by how much evidence each explains, not by authority — and that scientific conclusions can be revised as evidence accumulates.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence and is provisional: competing hypotheses are judged by how well they explain the evidence, and a genuine rival idea can still have supporters while the main case strengthens.

activities.title: Check your understanding of the case
feedback: A strong answer names the global impact winter and food-chain collapse reaching the whole planet, cites the iridium layer and Chicxulub crater, and notes that birds survived.
A partial answer names the asteroid, crater, or iridium layer but explains deaths by the direct blast and cannot describe the worldwide food-chain collapse — redirect to the aftermath activity.
A gap answer pictures the asteroid crushing or burning the dinosaurs with no global mechanism — reteach by separating the local impact from the global after-effects.
On the 'biggest extinction' probe: note that earlier extinctions (End-Permian) killed a far greater share of species; K-Pg is famous, not the largest.
activities.rationale: Recall and sorting tasks are useful companion checks that surface the specific misconceptions this topic targets. Such checks confirm whether learners can reproduce the argument; they do not, on their own, require learners to construct the argument, so they work best alongside the assembling and aftermath activities rather than replacing them.
learnerActions: Put the causal chain in the correct order: impact -> dust cloud -> less sunlight -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.

Sort clues into 'impact evidence' (e.g. worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age Chicxulub crater, iridium inside the crater) and items that are NOT impact evidence (e.g. an ordinary dinosaur fossil from older rock, a present-day volcanic rock, a river-worn pebble).
Answer why iridium is a clue (it is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids).

Answer the diagnostic question: 'An asteroid hit near Mexico ~66 Mya and most dinosaurs died. Did it kill them all just by crushing or burning them on impact? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.'

Respond to probes such as: since birds are living dinosaurs, is it right to say the asteroid killed ALL the dinosaurs? Why do plant-eaters die before meat-eaters? What evidence shows the effects reached the whole world? Was the K-Pg really the deadliest extinction ever?
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the age (~66 Mya), name the Chicxulub crater, cite the worldwide iridium layer, order the food-chain-collapse mechanism, and avoid the direct-killing, total-annihilation, and 'biggest-ever' misconceptions.

constraints: Target age 9-11. Anchor to fossils-as-evidence (UK Y3 Rocks, Y6 Evolution; NGSS 3-LS4-1), geologic time (MS-ESS1-4) and the working-scientifically/nature-of-science strand; there is no direct statutory KS2 dinosaur content.
Present clues first and let learners infer the cause; avoid announcing 'an asteroid did it' before the evidence is assembled.

Address the key misconceptions directly: most dinosaurs died from the global aftermath (impact winter, food-chain collapse) not the blast; birds are surviving dinosaurs so extinction was near-total not total; non-avian dinosaurs and humans did not overlap (separated by roughly 66 million years); the case rests on multiple independent evidence lines not one discovery; and the debate is not closed (the Deccan volcanism hypothesis, as a main cause or a contributor, still has supporters).

Recall/sorting checks assess whether learners can reproduce the argument but do not by themselves require independent construction of it; pair them with the evidence-assembling and aftermath activities, and populate both sort categories with real items so the task is a genuine discrimination.

A single annotated cross-section (tap-to-reveal: clay band = iridium from space, bones below, crater inset facts) is a useful scaffold for the boundary layer, but being fixed it does not let learners assemble the multi-clue argument or trace the cascade themselves — use it as support, not as the whole lesson.

Interaction examples (iridium meter that spikes, drill-core reveal, sunlight slider, sequential dimming of trophic levels, a wire linking crater to layer) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
Keep the distinction between the local impact (blast/heat near the crater) and the global after-effects (blocked sunlight worldwide) explicit so learners do not conflate them.

Distinguish the impact clues accurately: shocked quartz records intense shock pressure, while tektites are impact-melt droplets flung out by the impact's heat/energy — do not describe both as simply 'needing pressure.'
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the stated principle without proving any specific activity was tested.

Of the four source claims, only the UT Austin drill-core claim ('circle is now finally complete') is marked verified in the row; the Britannica, Wikipedia/Alvarez, and Science Advances claims are marked verified:false. Treat extinction percentages (~75–80%), the 'conclusively tying' language, and the characterisation of the Deccan rival as reported-but-unverified at this rewrite.

The source's 'circle is now finally complete' / 'conclusively tying' phrasing is strong; the rewrite presents the drill-core as closing only the link between crater and global layer, while the 'weigh the rival' activity preserves that a minority volcanism hypothesis persists, so the topic is not treated as fully closed.

Original research contained a non-preferred claim that '3D adds nothing' / depth 'adds cost without adding insight' and that dialogue 'cannot make tactile' the learning; these universal comparative claims are not established by the evidence and have been dropped or softened — a fixed cross-section and a researcher interview are retained as legitimate scaffolds/extensions with stated limits.

The original row grouped shocked quartz and tektites as both needing 'enormous pressure.' Shocked quartz forms under shock pressure, but tektites are impact-melt droplets formed by heat/energy and ejection; the corrected activity distinguishes them. This refinement was not re-verified against a fresh source.

Self-audit of the causal/biological logic found the mechanism (blocked sunlight -> photosynthesis crash -> herbivores before carnivores -> collapse), the local-vs-global distinction, the birds-survived point, and the End-Permian being larger than K-Pg to be internally consistent and retained as stated.

The ordering check in the final activity was aligned with the full taught chain (adding photosynthesis crash and ecosystem collapse) and the 'not impact evidence' sort category was populated with distractors so the classification task is performable.

probeDeeper: Birds are alive today and they are dinosaurs — so is it right to say the asteroid killed ALL the dinosaurs?
Why would plant-eaters die first and the meat-eaters soon after?
The crater is in Mexico. What evidence shows the effects reached the whole world?
Was the K-Pg really the deadliest extinction Earth has ever seen?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the impact itself only devastated the local area. Worldwide extinction came from the after-effects: dust and soot thrown into the sky blocked sunlight for years, so plants died, plant-eaters starved, and then the meat-eaters that fed on them starved — the food chain collapsed globally. Evidence includes the worldwide iridium layer and the Chicxulub crater.

errorPatterns.pattern: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs directly by hitting or burning them everywhere.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the local impact from the global aftermath — blocked sunlight, dying plants, collapsing food chains reaching animals far from Mexico.
errorPatterns.distractor: The asteroid crushed and burned all the dinosaurs when it hit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains worldwide death by the impact's blast/heat rather than by after-effects.

errorPatterns.pattern: It killed every single dinosaur — none survived at all.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Note that the non-avian dinosaurs died out but birds — living dinosaurs — survived; extinction was near-total, not total.
errorPatterns.distractor: It killed every single dinosaur, so no dinosaurs exist today.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States that no dinosaurs of any kind lived on, overlooking that birds are surviving dinosaurs.

errorPatterns.pattern: The K-Pg was the biggest extinction the Earth has ever had.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Mention that earlier extinctions (End-Permian) killed a far greater share of species; K-Pg is famous, not the biggest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Claims K-Pg was the deadliest ever, unaware of the larger End-Permian event.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the asteroid crushed or burned the dinosaurs directly, with no global mechanism.
responseLevels.full: Explains the impact-winter/food-chain-collapse mechanism reaching worldwide, cites the iridium layer and Chicxulub crater as evidence, and recognises birds survived.
responseLevels.partial: Knows an asteroid caused it and can name the crater or iridium layer, but explains the deaths by direct impact and cannot describe the worldwide food-chain collapse.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: About 66 million years ago an asteroid hit the Earth near Mexico and most dinosaurs died out. Did the asteroid kill all those dinosaurs just by crushing or burning them when it hit? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who pictures the asteroid as a giant direct killer says it flattened or burned the dinosaurs. A child who understands names the global 'impact winter' and food-chain collapse as the mechanism that reached the whole planet.
